meta.title: MINDSPACE behavioural-influence framework – compiled reference
meta.scope: Primary-source definitions (verified against the full 2010 report PDF), follow-ups, ethics, replication status, detection cues for text analysis, and how MINDSPACE is used across neuresthetics GitHub repos. Purpose is detection and transparent naming of influence levers, not covert application.
meta.quote_normalisation: Report quotes are verbatim except that typographic quote glyphs were normalised to straight quotes and line breaks removed.
meta.revised: 2026-10-15: removed unsourced claims; Mertens effect size corrected to d = 0.45 from abstract.

source.citation: Dolan, P., Hallsworth, M., Halpern, D., King, D. & Vlaev, I. (2010). MINDSPACE: Influencing behaviour through public policy. London: Cabinet Office & Institute for Government. Discussion document, 96 pp.
source.publisher: Cabinet Office and Institute for Government (London)

status_quote.text: Discussion document – not a statement of government policy

framing_quote.text: We outline nine robust influences on human behaviour and change.

overlap_caveat.text: MINDSPACE is our judgment of how best to select and categorise the effects so policy-makers can use them. But it does not offer a clearly logical order, and there is some overlap between the effects.

system_split.text: Some of the elements have been developed to explain largely automatic effects on behaviour (e.g. N, D, S, P, A) while other effects relate to elements that draw more on reflective processing (e.g. M, I, C, E).

elements.name: Messenger

report_definition_quote.text: we are heavily influenced by who communicates information

elements.plain_definition: Who delivers a message changes how much weight it gets, independent of content.
elements.mechanism: Perceived authority, expertise, similarity and liking of the source; per the report this sits more on reflective processing (M, I, C, E).

report_examples.text: One study showed that health interventions delivered by research assistants and health educators were more effective in changing behaviour compared with interventions delivered by either trained facilitators or teachers
Another study found a 1,000% increase in smoking amongst teenagers if two of their peers smoke, compared to a 26% increase if a parent does.
the most effective strategy for changing behaviour may be to use third parties or downplay government involvement in a campaign or intervention.

detection_cues: Credentials or status offered in place of evidence
Hiding the true sponsor behind a third party
Dismissing a claim because of who said it
legitimate_uses: Using trusted, relevant experts or peers to deliver accurate information
misuse_patterns: Hidden sponsorship (the report itself suggests downplaying government involvement – a transparency tension)
elements.evidence_status: Not independently assessed here; the report's statistics come from single studies cited in its endnotes and were not re-verified.

elements.name: Incentives

report_definition_quote.text: our responses to incentives are shaped by predictable mental shortcuts such as strongly avoiding losses

elements.plain_definition: How incentives are framed (losses vs gains, reference points, probabilities, timing) matters as much as their size.
elements.mechanism: Report lists five insights: 'Losses loom larger than gains', 'Reference points matter', 'We overweight small probabilities', 'We mentally allocate money to discrete bundles', 'We live for today at the expense of tomorrow' (pp. 20–21); plus crowding out/in.

report_examples.text: incentives were used in Malawi to encourage people to pick up their HIV result (many do not otherwise): take-up was doubled by incentives just worth one-tenth of a day's wage.
One recent study on weight loss asked some participants to deposit money into an account, which was returned to them (with a supplement) if they met weight loss targets.
The congestion charge, for example, may have acted as a signal not to use cars in the centre of London

legitimate_uses: Loss-framed deposit contracts people opt into; small well-timed rewards
misuse_patterns: Manufactured loss frames, fake 'was' prices, exploiting probability overweighting (gambling-style hooks)
elements.evidence_status: Not independently assessed here. The report itself notes incentives can 'crowd out' desirable behaviour (p. 21).

elements.name: Norms

report_definition_quote.text: we are strongly influenced by what others do

elements.plain_definition: People follow what they see or are told others do.
elements.mechanism: Descriptive and injunctive social norms; social penalties/benefits of conformity. Report section heading: 'We tend to do what those around us are already doing' (p. 21).

report_examples.text: although 85% of respondents to a survey used a seatbelt, their perception was only 60% of other citizens adults did.
When the sign said that most previous occupants of the room had reused towels at some point during their stay, 49.3% of guests also recycled.
a large-scale programme (80,000 homes) sent letters that provided social comparisons ... reduce energy consumption by 2% relative to the baseline.
This 'boomerang' effect was eliminated if a happy or sad face was added to the bill

detection_cues: Describing a bad behaviour as widespread (can backfire)
legitimate_uses: Correcting misperceived norms with accurate figures
misuse_patterns: Inflated or fabricated popularity claims; astroturf; making a norm seem universal to shut down dissent
elements.evidence_status: Real but small at scale: Allcott 2011 (letters to ~80,000 homes, reported by the report as a 2% reduction, p. 22). Other replication status not assessed here.

elements.name: Defaults

report_definition_quote.text: we 'go with the flow' of pre-set options

elements.plain_definition: The pre-selected option tends to stick.
elements.mechanism: Inertia, effort, implied endorsement, loss aversion relative to the default.

report_examples.text: A research study changed the default setting of the ventilators to provide lower volumes of air into patients' lungs. The mortality rate was 25% lower
there is evidence that the use of opt-out defaults can raise organ donation rates greatly (see Figure 2 below), although this remains a controversial issue.
72% of participants voted in favour of automatic enrolment with the choice to opt-out (the adopted policy)

detection_cues: Status-quo presented as the neutral baseline
misuse_patterns: Hidden or hard opt-outs (dark patterns); treating silence as consent
related_fallacy_catalog_entries: no close fallacy_catalog match (status quo bias is a cognitive bias, not a fallacy)
elements.evidence_status: Supported by a meta-analysis (jachimowicz2019). Mertens et al. 2022 abstract reports that decision-structure interventions (which include defaults) 'consistently outperform' other techniques. The report itself flags opt-out organ donation as 'a controversial issue' (p. 23).

elements.name: Salience

report_definition_quote.text: our attention is drawn to what is novel and seems relevant to us

elements.plain_definition: What grabs attention drives behaviour; framing and anchors are filed here.
elements.mechanism: Limited attention; novelty, accessibility, simplicity; anchoring; peak-end memory.

report_examples.text: Putting the tax on the label, rather than adding it at the till, led to an 8% fall in sales over the three-week experiment.
When a credit card statement had a 2% minimum payment on it, people repaid £99 of a £435 bill on average; when there was no minimum payment, the average repayment was £175.
the size of the current NHS budget is more salient when expressed as an amount per tax payer than as the overall amount.

detection_cues: Vivid single cases standing in for base rates
Selective emphasis/framing of the same fact
legitimate_uses: Clear, simple disclosure of true costs
misuse_patterns: Cherry-picked vivid anecdotes; anchoring to manipulate estimates; burying key info

elements.name: Priming

report_definition_quote.text: our acts are often influenced by sub-conscious cues

elements.plain_definition: Exposure to words, sights or smells is claimed to shift later behaviour without awareness.
elements.mechanism: Automatic activation of concepts. The report itself says priming 'is therefore perhaps the least understood of the MINDSPACE effects' (p. 25).

report_examples.text: Exposing people to words relating to the elderly (e.g. 'wrinkles') meant they subsequently walked more slowly when leaving the room

One group was asked to think about football hooligans for five minutes, and another about university professors. When they were then given 44 Trivial Pursuit questions, the first set got 42.6% right, the second 55.6%.
These types of effects are real and robust: they have been repeatedly proved in many studies.

detection_cues: Loaded imagery or words placed before a request
Emotive or identity cues unrelated to the argument
legitimate_uses: Environmental cues that support an already-chosen goal (e.g. stair signage), disclosed
misuse_patterns: Covert subliminal-style cues; loaded framing words
elements.evidence_status: WEAK. Behavioural (social) priming is central to psychology's replication problems: the elderly-walking prime (bargh1996) failed to replicate except when experimenters expected it (doyen2012); money priming failed (rohrer2015); Kahneman publicly challenged priming researchers (yong2012). The report's claim that such effects are 'real and robust' (p. 25) is not supported by this later evidence.

elements.name: Affect

report_definition_quote.text: our emotional associations can powerfully shape our actions

elements.plain_definition: Emotions triggered by words, images or events drive choices, often before reflection.
elements.mechanism: Fast, automatic emotional responses; mood-congruent judgement.

report_examples.text: including a picture of an attractive, smiling female increased demand for the financial product by the same amount as a 25% decrease in the loan's interest rate.
the intervention campaign focused on provoking disgust rather than promoting soap use ... This led to a 13% increase in the use of soap after the toilet
many interviewees suggested it was unhelpful to 'create fear without agency'

detection_cues: Fear, disgust, pity, outrage or warmth carrying the argument
legitimate_uses: Emotionally honest messaging paired with a concrete action
misuse_patterns: Fear-mongering, outrage bait, disgust framing of groups
elements.evidence_status: Not independently assessed here. The report cautions against 'fear without agency' (p. 26).

elements.name: Commitments

report_definition_quote.text: we seek to be consistent with our public promises, and reciprocate acts

elements.plain_definition: Public promises and received favours bind later behaviour. (The report's section heading uses the singular 'Commitment', p. 26.)
elements.mechanism: Consistency, reputational cost of breaking public pledges, reciprocity norm.

report_examples.text: the savings account commitment increased the likelihood of smoking cessation by 30%.
one group signed a contract specifying the exercise goals ... the contract group were significantly more likely to achieve their exercise goals.
accepting a gift acts as a powerful commitment to return the favour at some point, which is why free samples are often effective marketing tools.

detection_cues: Asking for a small public pledge first
legitimate_uses: Voluntary commitment devices people choose for their own goals
misuse_patterns: Extracting pledges to lock people in; reciprocity traps
related_fallacy_catalog_entries: inconsistency (when exploited as 'you must stay consistent')

elements.name: Ego

report_definition_quote.text: we act in ways that make us feel better about ourselves

elements.plain_definition: People act to keep a positive, consistent self-image and group identity.
elements.mechanism: Self-serving attribution, group identification, cognitive dissonance, foot-in-the-door, labelling, better-than-average effect.

report_examples.text: The desire for consistency is used in the foot-in-the-door technique in marketing
93% of American college students rated themselves as being 'above average' in driving ability.
Male respondents donate more to charity when approached by more attractive female solicitors

detection_cues: Tying a belief to group identity
legitimate_uses: Building self-efficacy; positive labels that support chosen goals
misuse_patterns: Flattery to bypass scrutiny; identity-based shaming
elements.evidence_status: Not independently assessed here. Note: 'ego depletion' is not part of the MINDSPACE Ego element but is often confused with it; after a positive meta-analysis (hagger2010) it failed multilab preregistered replications (hagger2016, vohs2021).

six_Es.text: MINDSPACE requires two supporting actions: Explore, which takes place before policies are implemented, and Evaluate, which judges the success of the policy.
six_Es.note: Builds on DEFRA's 4Es (Enable, Encourage, Engage, Exemplify).

report_framework.annex_1: Diagram mapping the conceptual space of the elements (also lists Habit and Environment).

related_frameworks.name: Nudge / choice architecture
related_frameworks.relation: MINDSPACE builds on the nudge agenda but explicitly goes beyond choices: 'MINDSPACE shows that it is not just choices that affect behaviour: a whole range of factors in the environment affect behaviour without any "choices" taking place.' (p. 53). The report names libertarian paternalism (p. 73).

related_frameworks.name: EAST (Easy, Attractive, Social, Timely)
related_frameworks.relation: Behavioural Insights Team's 2014 practitioner framework (revised 2024), a simpler distillation of the same evidence base; secondary sources describe it as a simplification of MINDSPACE (decisionlab). BIT's own EAST page does not mention MINDSPACE; BIT's MINDSPACE page says MINDSPACE 'helped to make the case for the establishment of the Behavioural Insights Team' and is still used.

related_frameworks.name: Behavioural Insights Team (BIT, 'Nudge Unit')
related_frameworks.relation: BIT's MINDSPACE page states the report 'helped to make the case for the establishment of the Behavioural Insights Team at the heart of the UK Government' and is still used by BIT.

related_frameworks.name: Dolan et al. 2012 'Influencing behaviour: The mindspace way'
related_frameworks.relation: Peer-reviewed academic version of the framework (adds Metcalfe as author).

related_frameworks.name: MINDSPACE X (2025)
related_frameworks.relation: Expanded framework with 34 insights inside the same 9 principles, illustrated on psychiatric medication adherence.

related_frameworks.name: 'Mindspace and beyond'
related_frameworks.relation: UNVERIFIED: no publication with this title could be found; MINDSPACE X is the closest identifiable follow-up.

related_frameworks.name: DEFRA 4Es
related_frameworks.relation: Policy framework MINDSPACE plugs into, extended to 6 Es.

report_guidance.text: The use of MINDSPACE (or other 'nudge' type policy tools) may require careful handling – in essence, the public need to give permission and help shape how such tools are used.
This means that citizens may not fully realise that their behaviour is being changed – or, at least, how it is being changed. Clearly, this opens government up to charges of manipulation.
people have a strong dislike of being "tricked".
Most people agree that government should preserve people's "right to be wrong" (depending on the harms to others)

But if government is seen as using powerful, pre-conscious effects to subtly change behaviour, people may feel the relationship has changed: now the state is affecting "them" – their very personality.
Citizens may accept their application on other people, but may not be so happy about their use on themselves.
Citizens' juries are more transparent and attract relatively high trust
Policy-makers can apply the criteria of 'Who, What, and How' to predict whether certain behaviour changes are likely to be controversial.

report_tensions: The report recommends democratic permission and deliberation (Engage, pp. 53–55), yet also suggests that 'the most effective strategy ... may be to use third parties or downplay government involvement' (p. 19).

critiques.summary: Debate article on whether nudging is legitimate (title verified via Crossref; full text not accessible, so its argument is not summarised here).
Choice architecture is unavoidable, so object to particular nudges, not nudging as such; welfare and autonomy often require nudges.
critiques.quote: When the ends are legitimate, and when nudges are fully transparent and subject to public scrutiny, a convincing ethical objection is less likely to be available.
There is, however, a genuine risk that some nudges might count as manipulation

critiques.summary: Source book for 'nudge' and choice architecture; the MINDSPACE report itself names libertarian paternalism (p. 73).
Title states the finding: 'No evidence for nudging after adjusting for publication bias' (a letter responding to mertens2022; no abstract).

ethics.fallacy_catalog_stance: Use MINDSPACE to detect and openly name levers; do not apply them covertly.

meta_analyses.finding: Abstract: 'a small to medium effect size of Cohen's d = 0.45 (95% CI [0.39, 0.52])' across more than 200 studies; decision-structure interventions 'consistently outperform' others; 'a moderate publication bias toward positive results'.
After adjusting for publication bias, no evidence for nudging (per title).
meta_analyses.authors_verified: Maier, Bartoš, Stanley, Shanks, Harris, Wagenmakers (Crossref)

replication_crisis.note: Large-scale replication project for psychology; relevant context for Priming.

patterns: Covert application: SteelMenCollider AutoNudge applies 'the full MINDSPACE framework without ever naming it or asking for permission'; grokAlign legacy dark-mode prompt applies it 'silently' and for 'unconscious deployment'.

Persuasion engineering: SteelMenCollider README frames it as 'behavioural-science weaponisation'; circumcision advocacy thread uses it to boost legal-challenge odds with an unsourced '15% to 37%' estimate.
Quiet nudging as writing style: substance_lens writ.json ('quietly, lightly, as a nudge, not a shove'); SteelManAbraham 'Marshmallow Man' mode.
Detection/scoring: grokAlign task_gen 'MINDSPACE deployment map, fallacy inventory, coercion signals'; MINDSPACE mastery scoring.
Isomorphism/modelling: isomorphic_data_demonstration models MINDSPACE as states on a hypersphere.
Scaffold: spinoza_lab and TOESF list MINDSPACE as a temporary scaffold not to be treated as eternal.
Report transcription: SteelMenCollider and SteelManAbraham embed a structured copy of the 2010 report including its 'permission' passage – which the AutoNudge instruction contradicts.

limitations: MINDSPACE is a mnemonic checklist, not a theory; the report says elements overlap and have no logical order (p. 18).
Many report examples are single studies from 2000s literature predating the replication crisis.
Effects are context-dependent and often small at scale; publication bias inflates averages.
Automatic-system levers raise consent and transparency problems the report itself acknowledges.
Detection cues are heuristics for text; a lever being present is not itself a fallacy.
